div.head: Chapter 28
div.p: The fourth cause of this right is to punish, chastise, and take vengeance for the said injuries, offenses, evils, and harms that they have received from the Spaniards, against natural, divine, and human law. And they are competent judges for this. For they can take action against criminal men and corrupters of their commonwealths, both internal ones — that is, their own citizens — and external ones — that is, those of another nation.
This is proved because they were and are kingdoms, peoples, or communities and free kings who recognize no superior in law, as was proved in the sixth principle, § 9.

For to every kingdom and community and free king there belongs, by natural, human, and divine law, the right to repel and prohibit everything that is harmful and corruptive of their political being, as appears above in the proof of this second conclusion; and this is done by punishing and taking vengeance for the injuries, offenses, and harms that evil men commit against such commonwealths. Now the Spaniards have been corrupters and destroyers of those kingdoms and communities and commonwealths, and of the entire political being they had in them, and have committed most grave injuries, offenses, and harms against those commonwealths, as the whole world ratifies. Therefore to the kingdoms and commonwealths and communities, and to the kings and lords to whom their care is entrusted, there belongs by natural, human, and divine law the right to punish them and take vengeance of them, and thus they are competent judges.

All of this is proved by the virtue of vindication, which has two acts. The first and principal is to punish and take vengeance for injuries already received. The second is the defense and repulsion of those that may be received. Whence Cicero, in the Rhetoric, says that "vindication is that by which force, injury, and in general whatever is obscure" — that is, ignominious — "is repelled by defending or avenging." This second act pertains also to any private person, namely: defense of oneself and of one's own, as is already clear from what was said above of Paul. The first, namely vindication or vengeance of injuries received by force, is the proper and exclusive act of the whole community, or of the one to whom the community has entrusted its care, because that one does something by whose authority it is done: see Dionysius, chapter 12 of the Celestial Hierarchy. And this is in a public person constituted in power — that is, representing the whole community or discharging its functions — and who holds the whole power and jurisdiction of the community. The reason is that to act or ordain something for the public good belongs to legal justice making use of commutative justice: since it renders to someone the equal and proportionate debt on account of the common good, and consequently it belongs to the community or to the public person. And so both on the part of the subject, and on the part of the quality of the debt, it appears that vindication is not a virtue in the singular person, but in public justice. For legal justice does not pertain to the singular person but to the public person, because to do what is due in order to the community and to avoid the opposite evil belongs to general or legal justice, and pertains to the whole community or the public person. And so one of the actions or effects of law is the punishment of wrongdoers, as is evident from the Decrees, 3 Dist., c. fin. et from Isidore, 2 Etymologies; et Saint Thomas, 1.2 q. 9 a. 2 corp.; but to enact laws belongs to the community or to the one to whom the care of preserving the community is entrusted. Therefore. And that punishment or vengeance for wrongdoers pertains to the community or to the one who acts in its place is not in doubt.

And this is confirmed by Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 40 a. 1 corp., where he says that since the care of the commonwealth is entrusted to princes, it is their task to protect the commonwealth of the city, kingdom, or province entrusted to them. And so they lawfully defend it with the material sword against internal disturbers when they punish wrongdoers, according to that passage of Romans 13: "For he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is God's minister: an avenger to execute wrath upon the one who does evil." And likewise with the sword of war it is their task to protect the commonwealth from external enemies. Thus from him. And on the virtue of vindication, see what the same Doctor teaches in 2.2, q. 108, throughout.

Since, therefore, those communities or free peoples were and are free, and their princes and lords to whom their care was entrusted by those same communities from ages past, were able and are able to enact laws, by virtue of having full power and jurisdiction, pure and mixed authority by natural law and the law of nations, and it falls to them to compel and ordain everything that is fitting for the common good and for avoiding evil, and to protect those commonwealths from enemies and corrupters: and the Spaniards have been their most fierce enemies and destroyers or exterminators of those peoples and of innumerable communities, whom they have afflicted with so many thousands of injuries, killings, massacres, torments, despoilings, servitude, and irreparable harms: it follows that they can and must proceed against them with the sword of war, and avenge all the injuries and harms they have suffered from them, punishing the delinquents, criminals, and pernicious men with death, captivity, despoiling, expulsion from the homeland, and from the foreign kingdoms they have tyrannically occupied. Indeed, even given the case — which is false — that those nations had recognized our king as their superior, as we proved in principle 6, it would still have been and would be lawful for them to wage war against the Spaniards, their enemies, and against the judges, governors, or officials of the king, and to kill them and drive them from their lands and kingdoms, and to obtain justice for their harms and injuries through war or by whatever other means they could. This is proved because never in that land, nor in other parts of the Indies, was justice administered to them; rather the governors and judges of our king were still more pernicious and unjust and harmful — more cruel tyrants, in fact —, and through their ambition and greed the peoples of the Indies perished and perish each day. Now wherever and whenever a just judge is not available, whether in law — because they are free peoples — or in fact — because the superior does not do or refuses, and does not want to, or conceals, or neglects to do justice —, which is the same as if no one existed, because not to exist and to exist uselessly are judged equal, as in cap. 2, De translatione prelatorum; or if imminent necessity gives no time to approach a judge because of the danger of delay, and no recourse to the king or superior can be had; or if necessity urges in some other way; or also where rights are trampled with reckless presumption by the power of the one who commits the injustice, or inflicts the injury and the wrong, and in brief wherever justice cannot be secure: it is lawful for anyone or all to whom it matters, even those who recognize a superior, to take up arms by their own authority and declare war — namely, a war of defense. For then not the individual or the individuals act, but natural law, by whose authority they act. Whence, against one who deviates from the key of justice, there is no remedy but the armed hand, as Baldo well says in L. data opera, Codex, De his qui accusare non possunt, penult. col. and he cites L. ut vim, ff., De Justitia et jure et in L. si quis ad se, Codex, Ad legem Juliam et vi publica. And this is an extensive matter treated principally in L. prohibitum, Codex, De jure fisci., Lib. 10, where see Bartolus, etc.

Those peoples therefore have, with or without their natural kings and lords, the most powerful right to declare war against the Spaniards, by reason of avenging the most grave crimes that have been committed against them.

They also have just war, for the fifth cause, against them: for the cause of necessity, in order to acquire or defend the peace, health, liberty, and life of many, etc. This cause is included in the others, or it itself comprehends all the aforementioned causes within it, and is clear in itself; therefore no more will be said of it here.

Second part of the second conclusion. It is stated in the conclusion — and so is its second part — that they had just war against all the Spaniards. This is proved: first, because regarding all the Spaniards who dwell in those lands and flock to them every day, all the peoples of that entire world have the very long experience that they intend nothing but to subjugate them through wars, massacres, and killings of men, and to impose upon them their iron yoke and the most abject servitude, in which some are exterminating entire communities, and they know with certainty that vast provinces and kingdoms once most fully peopled have been perversely depopulated by their abominable and more than wicked crimes. Second, because although some Spaniard may not go there with such a purpose — which must be attributed to a great miracle — and may not in truth have inflicted any harm on them, nonetheless, since such persons are extremely few, they are not held to be free of blame: the presumption against them is vehement and just, against all and each one, and therefore the sentence of military justice is not bound to discern whether any or some portion of the republic that is its enemy may be innocent, because the whole is presumed to be enemy, and the whole is held as enemy, and therefore the whole is condemned and destroyed. And on this we have said much elsewhere, and the Doctors treat it; seek it therefore elsewhere.
